onboarding-interview-a.txt:
Synthetic acceptance interview A. The researcher entered a new project and expected an obvious place to import interview notes. The first screen did not explain whether a project was an empty folder or a running research job. The researcher looked at the mission controls before finding the document area, then asked whether importing a file would start a paid run. A short explanation of what an upload changes would have made that choice easier. The participant wanted the current project name beside the upload action and a clear confirmation naming the destination after the file appeared.

The participant also struggled to distinguish a collection from a project. They thought saving an excerpt might move the original document out of its project. During the session they asked for a preview showing the collection name, its destination Space, the source document and the exact excerpt to be saved. They wanted each source link to remain visible after saving so another researcher could reopen the surrounding text. Their suggested wording was that a collection gathers references while the original research stays where it is. The researcher preferred choosing a small group of related passages over automatically filing every document.

When shown a possible summary, the participant checked the source of each claim before deciding whether to keep it. They asked for a report preview that remains the same when saved. A second generation step would make their review feel wasted because a sentence or citation could change after approval. They wanted the saved report to include the question they had asked and a clear indication of whether they had edited the proposed text. The ability to export the same citations was more useful to this participant than changing the visual report template.

The researcher returned to the collection after navigating to a source document. They expected their proposed name and selected members to survive that navigation. They also expected an interrupted save to show which excerpts were already added and which were still missing. Starting a second collection with the same name would be confusing because they would not know which one to use. For a retry, the participant wanted to finish the first collection and receive one link to its completed view. They did not request automatic deletion, retagging, document moves, shared access, background organisation or a new search system. These notes are controlled fixtures rather than findings from an actual participant.
onboarding-interview-b.txt:
Synthetic acceptance interview B. The participant opened a project containing several documents and looked for a guide to the next useful action. They wanted to bring their own field notes into the project before asking a research question. The import action was not easy to locate from the project header. They hesitated because the nearby mission button sounded like it might start research immediately. A visible project label and a short upload confirmation were their main requests. They also wanted a clear distinction between adding existing material and commissioning a new research run.

The participant planned to organise feedback by pain point. They wanted to inspect a suggested collection before creating it, rename it in familiar terms, and remove any excerpt that did not help answer their question. They did not want a collection suggestion to change the source documents or alter existing tags. The order of excerpts mattered because they wanted to read an observation before the explanation of its effect. The participant proposed an initial collection about unclear navigation, followed by a separate group about trust in saved research. They wanted to accept these groups one at a time rather than approve a batch.

The source links made a proposed group more credible. The participant clicked an excerpt to see its original document and surrounding context, then returned to the proposal. They expected the same project and proposed membership to remain selected. A label saying that only part of the project had been read would help them understand why some documents were absent. They were comfortable with a small sample if the application named the sample and avoided claiming to have reviewed the entire library. They wanted unprocessed material to remain visibly distinct from excerpts that were ready for analysis.

For reporting, the participant wanted a concise synthesis of the collection they had just reviewed. They asked to see the source of each factual paragraph and to edit the title before saving. They expected the saved report and its export to retain the same wording and numbered citations. They did not ask the assistant to publish the report or share the underlying project. When a save failed halfway through, their preference was to retry the missing work in the existing destination. A duplicate collection would add uncertainty about which version was complete. Their comments supported explicit previews, stable source identities and small recoverable actions. This document is a synthetic test fixture and must not be presented as real participant research.
onboarding-interview-c.txt:
Synthetic acceptance interview C. The researcher had interview notes ready to upload but could not quickly tell which project would receive them. They moved between the project page and the document list looking for an import control. A destination label beside the action would have reduced that uncertainty. They wanted the resulting message to confirm the document name and project instead of showing only a generic success state. The researcher also asked for help understanding the difference between creating a research mission and adding their existing notes to the library.

The researcher then reviewed a suggestion to group passages about onboarding friction. They preferred a short collection name that described the question the passages could answer. They wanted an editable description explaining why those passages belonged together. Exact membership was more useful than a vague promise to organise all feedback. They asked to remove one irrelevant passage while keeping the other members in their current order. Saving the group should create a new collection with the reviewed name and members. It should not rename existing collections or move documents into another Space.

The participant used source links to check whether a suggested theme was supported. They wanted the link to open the selected excerpt directly, with enough document context to understand it. After returning, the proposal should remain available without another model request. They also wanted to know whether the analysis included all available excerpts or only a bounded sample. Empty files and materials without usable text should not count as evidence that the assistant had read. The researcher said they would rather see a clear gap than a confident description of material that had never reached the model.

A report assembled from the reviewed collection was the final useful step for this participant. They wanted the assistant to draft it, let them inspect citations, and save the exact preview only when asked. They expected the saved artifact to identify the source project and retain the original prompt. If the collection contained unrelated project material, they wanted the application to show the eligible subset before drafting. They also requested a useful retry after interrupted saves, including a link to any collection already created and a count of missing excerpts. They did not request autonomous background work, duplicate deletion, source rewriting or broader sharing permissions. This is a controlled synthetic interview used to verify the application workflow, not a claim about a real researcher.
